quiz_question: A budding gymnast of mass, M = 55.0 kg does a hand stand, pushing vertically down on a balance beam at a distance d = 2.32 m from the LEFT support of a uniform balance beam of length L = 2.90 m and mass m = 11.0 kg. What is the magnitude of the force exerted by the LEFT support on the beam? Magnitude of acceleration due to gravity is 10 m/s2. Select the closest answer.
essay: I would find the average net force on the ball by the wall by first understanding that in order to find the force on the ball by the wall, you need to use the known distance and avergae velocity to find the time it takes for the ball to be compressed. Then you can rearrange the distance equation solving for net force, since distance, mass, initial velocity, and time are known. then divide the net force by 2 to find the avaerage net force.
feedback-a: You don't need to compute the time here; using average velocity requires constant acceleration, and dividing a computed net force by two is not justified. Instead, relate the change in kinetic energy to the work done over the compression distance to get the magnitude of the average force. Alternatively, if you assume constant deceleration, use the stopping distance and initial speed to find the deceleration via kinematics, then obtain the force from mass times deceleration and treat it as the average wall force without any extra division.
feedback-b: Base your approach on the momentum/impulse principle rather than trying to extract force from a distance equation, and define the ball as the system with the wall as the surroundings while neglecting gravity during the short collision. Use the fact that the ball comes to rest to determine the momentum change, and obtain the collision time from the compression distance and the average of the initial and final speeds. Then relate that momentum change to the average net force over the collision time—there is no extra division by two.

essay: If a ball of known mass is traveling at a known speed smashes into a wall and comes to rest momentarily and we know that the ball compressed a known distance, we could find the avergae net force exerted on the ball by the wall by first calculating the initial and final momentum of the ball before and after hitting the wall and also calculating the distance that the ball compressed. We also use the initial and final velocities of the ball in these calculations to get ourselves the answer to these problems. Therefore, this is how we can calculate the net force exerted on ball by wall. We'll also use the time in the calculation.
feedback-a: Avoid the momentum/impulse route here because you are not given the contact time. Use energy instead: as the ball goes from its initial speed to rest over the compression distance, the lost kinetic energy equals the work done by the average wall force. Treat the force as roughly constant during that short compression, take the final speed as zero, and you can ignore gravity over the brief impact.
feedback-b: Use the Momentum Principle: the average force is determined by how quickly the ball’s momentum changes. Since the ball stops, the change in momentum equals its initial momentum, and you still need the collision time, which you can find from the compression distance and the ball’s average speed during compression (halfway between its starting speed and zero if the slowing is roughly uniform). State your assumptions clearly (approximately constant force during compression and negligible gravity) so this approach is valid.

Additionally, you will need the length of time that the ball was in contact with the ball and the distance that the ball was compressed. Once you know all of this information, you can find the change in momentum. Finally, the change in momentum divided by the duration of the impact (also known as change in time) would result in the net force of the collision.
feedback-a: You don’t need the contact time here; use the energy perspective by equating the loss of kinetic energy to the work done over the compression distance to get the average force. If you prefer momentum methods, first infer a constant deceleration from the given speed and stopping distance, then obtain the contact time and proceed. During such a brief impact, you can neglect weight so the wall’s average force effectively equals the net force on the ball.
feedback-b: Make the Momentum Principle explicit for the ball as the system, with the wall as the only significant external force; neglect gravity over the brief contact and justify using a roughly constant (average) force. You don’t need the contact time provided; determine it from the compression distance using the average speed during the slowdown, which is the mean of the initial and final speeds. Then compute the momentum change magnitude and use it over that derived time to obtain the average force.
